meta.title: Who really said "Don't be afraid to give up the good to go for the great"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Rockefeller. Wikiquote files it as disputed: the earliest print credit goes to Kenny Rogers, and nobody credited Rockefeller before 2006.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Don't be afraid to give up the good to go for the great'?
meta.ogDescription: It is not in Rockefeller's 1909 memoir and nobody cites a speech or letter. The paper trail starts in a 1990s quote anthology crediting Kenny Rogers.

answer.label: Not John D. Rockefeller — origin unknown
answer.authorDates: Author unidentified · earliest located print credit: Kenny Rogers (1938–2020)
answer.sourceLine: Nobody has produced a source. The line is absent from Rockefeller’s own memoir, Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (Doubleday, Page & Company, 1909) — searchable in full at Project Gutenberg ↗ — and the sites that circulate it name no speech, letter or book. Wikiquote files it under Disputed: the earliest printed instance it located credits country singer Kenny Rogers, and no attribution to Rockefeller appears until 2006 Wikiquote, Disputed ↗. Rogers is the oldest credit, not a proven author — so the honest answer is unknown.

source.excerpt: Don’t be afraid to give up the good to go for the great.
trail: The anchor is Wikiquote, which does not list this line among Rockefeller’s quotes at all — it files it under Disputed, noting that the earliest citation it found in Google Books is from 1993, where the line is credited to country-music singer Kenny Rogers, and that it is not found attributed to Rockefeller until 2006 the Disputed entry ↗.

We followed both volumes Wikiquote links. The earliest one is Words of Wisdom, an advice-and-quotation anthology compiled by William Safire and Leonard Safir for Simon and Schuster Google Books record ↗. The first Rockefeller credit sits in Networking in 90 Minutes by Lindsay Bannerman, published by White Finance Ltd in 2006 Google Books record ↗. Both are books repeating a credit, which is not the same thing as a source.

We searched Rockefeller’s end ourselves. His memoir Random Reminiscences of Men and Events — Doubleday, Page & Company, 1909, copyright 1908 and 1909 — is online in full, and it contains no ‘give up the good’, no ‘go for the great’ and no ‘afraid to give’ the full text ↗. Rockefeller died in 1937; the line has no printed life under any name until the 1990s.

The specialists have not rescued it either. Quote Investigator has traced four separate sayings pinned on Rockefeller — blood in the streets, compound interest, the pessimist and the optimist, and ‘I believe the market is going to fluctuate’ — and this is not one of them QI’s Rockefeller file ↗. Wikiquote’s Kenny Rogers page ↗ does not carry the line either, so even the oldest credit has nothing behind it.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller passage to show, because there is no passage — the line only ever appears as a free-standing motto. One wrinkle worth flagging: Wikiquote’s note dates its earliest Google Books hit to 1993, while Google Books’ own record for the volume Wikiquote links gives a publication date of April 1990. Either way the trail begins in a 1990s quotation anthology crediting Kenny Rogers, not in anything Rockefeller wrote.
source.rightsNote: We cannot state a rights position, because we cannot state an author or a first publication. The earliest appearances anyone has located are in modern, in-copyright books — a Simon and Schuster anthology and a 2006 networking handbook — and both of those are repeating the line, not originating it. So do not treat this as public domain on the strength of Rockefeller’s 1839–1937 dates: nothing ties it to him or to any pre-1931 work. Quote it in a talk or a card; do not print it on merchandise under a dead man’s name. This is not legal advice.

author.name: John D. Rockefeller
author.kicker: The name it gets pinned to
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Rockefeller
author.bio: John Davison Rockefeller founded and led the Standard Oil Company and then gave away a fortune through the Rockefeller Foundation, the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research and the University of Chicago. He did write about his own career — Random Reminiscences of Men and Events, published by Doubleday, Page & Company in 1909 — which is why this attribution is easy to test, and why it fails: the book is online in full and the words are not in it. What he is remembered for, ploughing returns back into the business rather than pocketing them, is close enough to the sentiment that the misattribution feels plausible; feels plausible is not a source.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is a motivational-poster line wearing a robber baron’s name. Rockefeller is the perfect host for it — rich, ruthless, dead, and permanently associated with reinvesting profits — but the paper trail runs the other way, and it does not start with him.

items.why: Wikiquote does not list it among his quotes; it sits in the Disputed section with no Rockefeller attribution located before 2006 the entry ↗. It is also absent from his own memoir, and none of the business sites repeating it cite a speech, letter or book — one concedes that “attribution can vary across sources” an example ↗.

Wikiquote’s earliest Google Books instance credits the country singer Wikiquote ↗, and quotation sites still list a shorter form under his name. But an anthology repeating a credit is not evidence he wrote it, and his own Wikiquote page ↗ does not include it.

The oldest Rockefeller attribution anyone has located is in Networking in 90 Minutes by Lindsay Bannerman, White Finance Ltd, 2006 Google Books ↗. From there it spread through quote databases, where Goodreads now carries it under his name with no source at all Goodreads ↗.

items.who: Jim Collins — 'Good is the enemy of great'
items.why: The sentiment’s best-known respectable version is Collins’s own line from Good to Great, which he states plainly and which is properly his Collins on it ↗. It is a much later formulation than the anonymous motto on this page, but it is why the idea now reads as business scripture.

misattribution.truthLine: Unknown. The oldest credit belongs to Kenny Rogers, the Rockefeller credit begins in 2006, and Rockefeller’s own book does not contain the words the trail ↗.

context.heading: Why it sticks
lead: The line works because it names a real and uncomfortable trade. Most people are not choosing between failure and success; they are choosing between something that already works and something that might work better, and the thing that already works is the harder one to walk away from. Naming ‘the good’ as the obstacle is the whole trick.

It also explains the Rockefeller magnetism. Reinvesting rather than banking a profit is the single idea most associated with him, so a motto about surrendering a comfortable return sounds like something he would say — which is exactly the mechanism by which unsourced aphorisms acquire famous owners.
context.detailsSummary: Why a famous name gets attached to a sourceless line
detailsBody: A motto with no author looks weak on a slide. A motto with a titan’s name looks like evidence, so a name gets supplied.
The name supplied is nearly always someone the audience already accepts on the subject. For money and ambition in English, that means Rockefeller, Ford or Carnegie.
The direction of travel here is unusual and instructive: the line lost a living, checkable credit (a singer, in a 1990s anthology) and gained a dead, unfalsifiable one.
‘Unknown’ is the correct answer, and it is more useful than a confident wrong one — particularly if you were about to print it.
context.pull: Naming ‘the good’ as the obstacle is the whole trick.
